about.title: Placentia Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Placentia's mix of warehouses, retail centers, and commercial stretches along Orangethorpe Avenue and Placentia Avenue means workplace injuries happen in all sorts of settings — from delivery drivers navigating SR-57 on-ramps to workers on job sites near busy intersections. In California, workers' compensation is generally the exclusive path for claims against your own employer, no matter who was at fault. But when a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to your injury, you may also have a separate third-party claim worth exploring. Orange County's job sites and delivery routes create real overlap between workplace safety and traffic risk, especially for anyone working near Placentia's higher-volume corridors. LawProactive doesn't practice law — we simply connect injured workers with independent attorneys who can look at the full picture, sort out which claims apply, and explain your options at no upfront cost. Reporting your injury promptly matters, so don't wait to get informed.

whyChoose.title: Why Placentia Workers Look Into Their Options

items.title: Workers' Comp Isn't Always the Whole Story
items.desc: California law generally makes workers' comp the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party — like a subcontractor or equipment maker — can still be liable separately.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Matter
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and a separate 2-year deadline applies to third-party injury claims, so timing counts.

items.title: Retaliation Is Illegal
items.desc: California law protects you from being fired or punished for reporting a workplace injury, which means you can pursue a claim without fear of losing your job for doing so.

items.question: Can I file a claim if I was hurt on a delivery route near SR-57 in Placentia?
items.answer: Possibly, yes. If another driver caused the crash while you were working, you may have both a workers' comp claim and a separate third-party claim against that driver. An independent attorney can review the details and explain which options fit your situation.

items.question: Does workers' comp cover everything, or can I sue my employer too?
items.answer: In most cases, workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer, meaning you generally can't sue them separately even if they were careless. However, if someone outside your employer — like a subcontractor or manufacturer — contributed to your injury, a third-party claim may still be available.

items.question: What if my employer retaliates after I report an injury?
items.answer: California law prohibits retaliation against workers who report workplace injuries, including firing, demotion, or other punishment. If this happens, it's worth discussing with an attorney, since it may open up additional legal options beyond your original injury claim.
